title: Spline shafts: How to specify, verify, and source parts that actually mate
summary: Spline shafts can pass inspection and still bind at assembly. Learn how to specify fit, tolerance class, and verification to get parts that mate.
body_markdown:
Your spline shaft passed inspection, and the material and heat-treatment records are in order. Then the hub binds during insertion. Or the parts assemble easily, with rotational clearance your design can’t tolerate.


A spline shaft transmits torque through mating teeth on a shaft and hub, either as a fixed joint or with axial float.


Tooth thickness may be the first dimension checked, although pitch error can change regional clearances and conceal them. Heat treatment may also distort the spline, relative to a bearing journal or the hub mating feature. A shaft can therefore have an acceptable


*local* tooth measurement, and still present a fit or alignment problem at assembly.


A production drawing must define the mating geometry with enough precision for the supplier to manufacture and inspect, not requiring supplementing critical details from experience.


Engineering drawing detail of a spline shaft callout showing standard, pitch, teeth, pressure angle, fit type, and tolerance class.


## Spline types and where they are used


The majority of production splines are either involute, crowned, or straight-sided, though other forms can be utilized. Serrated V form, helical, tapered, square, and ball splines are also used, for varied benefits.


The three main tooth forms are shown above, though many dimensional, angular and radius variants apply even to these.


Involute splines use curved tooth flanks, derived from involute geometry. They are common in transmissions, gearboxes and actuators, particularly where a standardized flank fit and established inspection system are beneficial.


Straight-sided splines have substantially parallel tooth flanks. They are common on legacy machinery. They are also simpler to machine than involute forms. ISO 14 covers straight-sided splines for cylindrical shafts with circumferential centering that the standard refers to as


*internal centering* .


For replacement work, the mating component (if undamaged) usually settles the choice. A shaft intended for an installed population of hubs needs to retain the spline system used by those hubs, where the connection is not being respecified.


Crowned splines are more specialized. A small longitudinal modification to the tooth form can reduce contact stress concentration near the ends of the engagement, when minor angular misalignment is a risk. The degree of crown depends heavily on the expected misalignment, and the engagement geometry. Excessive crowning reduces the available contact area, which may require compensating changes in tooth geometry.


## Flank fit and diameter centering


Many involute spline systems rely on contact between the mating tooth flanks for centering. A diameter-centered spline uses a cylindrical spline diameter to establish concentricity, so the drawing and inspection method must reflect this co-location.


Consider a transmission shaft running between two precision bearing journals. The bearings establish the operating axis, so the spline may need a runout requirement referenced to those journals, to prevent binding induced by competing centers. Meeting the spline tooth limits must not control the centering relationship.


Similar problems occur where a spline sits within a gear seat or seal circumference. The datum scheme should follow the mode in which the shaft is supported and located in service. In many such setups, a runout requirement between the spline and journal has more functional value than tightening an isolated spline diameter.


Side (flank) fit vs major-diameter fit. In side fit, the flanks contact and center the parts, with clearance at the tooth tips. Side fit is the standard fit for involute splines, which are self-centering (PartMFG; Engineers Edge). In major-diameter fit, the major diameter sets concentricity.


## Standards and spline designation


The standard applicable carries much of the spline definition, and should be clearly shown on the drawing and associated manufacturing information.


[ANSI/SAE B92.1](https://www.scribd.com/document/390049842/ANSI-B92-1-1996-Involute-Splines-and-Inspection) is widely used for inch, involute splines. Its involute systems include 30°, 37.5° and 45° pressure angles, with provisions for the fits and dimensional controls used on mating internal and external splines. B92.1 defines three fit types: flat-root side fit, fillet-root side fit and major-diameter fit (Hexagon WN4; Engineers Edge). Hexagon WN4 calls the third type “major diameter side fit. By convention, the internal spline is held to basic dimensions and the external spline is varied to control the fit (Engineers Edge). In practice, the fit you choose is set on the shaft.


[ISO 4156](https://www.iso.org/obp/ui/es/#iso:std:iso:4156:-1:ed-2:v1:en:fig:15) covers metric straight cylindrical involute splines with side fit. It also includes 30°, 37.5° and 45° nominal pressure-angle systems.


[DIN 5480](https://www.scribd.com/document/467384801/DIN-5480-3-Involute-Spline-Joints) is a metric involute system based on reference diameters and 30° pressure-angle geometry. A DIN 5480 designation cannot be converted to ISO 4156 simply by retaining a similar module and tooth count. The systems define geometry and tolerances in divergent ways.DIN 5480 covers modules 0.5–10 and uses primarily flank centering (diameter centering permitted as an exception), per DIN 5480-1 and DIN 5480-2:2015. If your drawing calls out DIN 5480, the hub and the gauges have to be DIN 5480 too.


[ISO 14](https://www.iso.org/standard/3596.html) covers straight-sided splines with internal centering.


Problems tend to arise when the drawing carries the required standard designation, but downstream documents reduce the feature to a nominal diameter and tooth count. Inspection then lacks a secure basis for selecting which fit or tooth-size limits apply. Retaining the original spline designation on the purchase order AND inspection plan avoids the risk of degraded definition.


## What the drawing has to define


The selected standard determines the exact designated format. The drawing will normally identify tooth count and pitch or module, together with the pressure angle and fit information required by that system. The corresponding tooth-thickness or space-width limits follow from the standard and tolerance designation, rather than being directly dimensioned on the drawing.


Usable spline length requires separate attention, as it is possible for nominal


*cut length* and


*working engagement* to become conflated.


For example, if the hub requires 30 mm of full-form engagement, dimensioning 30 mm from the front of the spline to a shoulder is unlikely to provide it. The entry chamfer consumes some length, and the cutting tool may leave an incomplete form as it approaches the shoulder. The resulting full-form region could be significantly shorter than the dimension suggests.


Tool access should be considered at the same point. A hob needs clearance to generate the tooth near the end of the cut. Shaper processing and grinding each impose their own approach and runout issues. If the design places full-depth teeth directly against a shoulder, an undercut or relief is advisable. Occasionally the geometry forces a different spline process than the one originally specified.


Internal splines can be more restrictive. A broach needs a through path, so a blind spline cannot simply inherit a process selected for an otherwise similar


*through* bore.


The drawing also has to connect the spline to the rest of the shaft. Bearing journals may establish the datum axis; a locating shoulder or sprung clip may establish axial position. The spline callout itself does not directly control either relationship.


A callout containing only:


**24T INVOLUTE SPLINE**


leaves the supplier without a governing standard, pitch or module, pressure angle, fit or tolerance basis.


The production callout should use the full designation prescribed by the applicable standard. Shaft-specific dimensions can then deal with engagement length, spline termination, and the datum relationship to adjacent features. Heat treatment requirements, and final surface condition also belong on the drawing, when they affect acceptance.


## The internal spline has to be considered at the same time


External tooth thickness and internal space width are defined within the same mating tolerance system.


This can be overlooked when the shaft and hub are sourced separately. Nominal CAD geometry may show ample clearance, but the useful calculation is the permitted fit, across the tolerance limits of


*both* components. Sliding splines require enough clearance to move under the expected operating conditions. A fixed connection will have quite different requirements.


Replacement production exposes weak specifications quickly. A shaft produced five years after the original hub should still assemble, if both parts conform to the same definition. If the assembly requires trial of several shafts before finding one that fits, selective assembly has effectively entered the production process. This highlights variability either in the new part or the legacy component.


Engagement length is also a critical mating characteristic. Only the portion of the teeth actually


*engaged* by the hub can contribute directly to the connection. A longer available engagement length on the shaft adds value in special conditions, such as a sliding joint.


## Actual tooth size and effective fit


An external spline can pass a tooth-thickness inspection, yet fail to enter a conforming internal spline.


One common cause of this is pitch error. Each tooth may have an acceptable local thickness, yet small positional errors around the circumference cause several teeth to contact their mating spaces prematurely. Lead or profile error can produce a similar disruptive outcome.


Spline inspection therefore distinguishes


*actual* tooth size from


*effective fit.* These quantities account for geometrical variation that is not evident in a single local tooth-size measurement. Effective tooth thickness adds the effect of form errors to the actual thickness, and the effective value decides whether your parts assemble (DIN 5480-1, §10.6). ANSI B92.1 absorbs profile tolerance into composite tooth thickness (CTT) on external splines and composite space width (CSW) on internal splines (ANSI B92.1)


An effective inspection plan typically specifies analytical information about the tooth size, and a validation check for functional engagement, as a go-no-go gauge.


### Measurement over pins or balls


Pins or balls provide a practical analytical measurement because direct measurement of an involute flank is awkward with conventional shop equipment.


For an external spline, pins of the specified diameter are seated in tooth spaces and the dimension over them is measured. Internal splines can use corresponding between-pin or ball methods where the spline standard provides for them. Pin size, and the resulting acceptance dimensions, are derived from the standards-based spline geometry.


During machining, successive over-pin measurements can indicate progressive cutter wear, before the tooth-size limit is reached.


The pins contact only selected tooth spaces. Pitch error elsewhere around the circumference will have little effect on that reading. A full-form gauge examines engagement across the spline and is commonly used alongside the analytical measurement, where effective fit mist be precisely controlled.


## Functional GO and NO-GO gauging


A full-form GO gauge engages multiple teeth simultaneously. Accumulated pitch error can then affect entry even when local tooth-size measurements remain acceptable.


The spline standard determines the exact relationship between GO, NO-GO and analytical limits. The inspection plan must identify which characteristic each method is appropriate to, along with the gauge class and any calibration requirements.


Production hubs sometimes find their way onto the inspection bench as convenient assembly checks. They can help diagnose a problem, but their own manufacturing tolerance makes them unsuitable as master acceptance gauges. Wear may even add an uncontrolled variable, once the same hub has been used many times.


Functional gauging for an external spline. The full-form GO ring gauge must assemble over the spline and checks the effective (maximum-material) limit, including accumulated pitch and lead error. The sector NO-GO gauge must not enter and checks the actual tooth-thickness limit. Measurement over pins can check the actual limit too. Internal splines follow the same logic with GO and NO-GO plug gauges (DIN 5480-1, §10.12).


### CMM and dedicated spline inspection


A CMM can measure pitch and inspect the spline relative to the shaft datum structure. With appropriate software and probing, it can also provide profile and lead information.


The limiting issue is measurement capability. A CMM report containing many decimal places can be informative, but may still leave uncertainties. Probe access and sampling strategy can have a substantial effect on spline results, especially on small teeth or short engagement lengths.


Dedicated gear and spline measuring equipment may be justified, where those characteristics are critical or production volume is high. Simpler gauges can still be the better production control for a functional limit, if they reproduce the relevant mating condition sufficiently well.


## Manufacturing route


Hobbing is a common choice for external splines, wherein the cutter has sufficient approach and overrun space. It is productive and well suited to high volume throughput.


Shaping becomes useful around geometry that restricts hob access. CNC milling can suit low quantities, replacement shafts and unusual tooth forms, where dedicated tooling would overwhelm the cost of the job.


Internal spline economics look different. Broaching can produce through splines very quickly, but the broach is expensive dedicated tooling. At high volume that investment may be easy to justify, whereas at low volume it can cost more than the parts. Blind internal splines remove the possibility of broaching, generally requiring shaper or skiving methods.


Cold rolling forms the teeth plastically. The resulting surface can be very good, and the compressive residual stress generated by forming can improve fatigue performance. Tooling economics generally limit rolling to higher-volume production.


Grinding is commonly used after hardening, when the final tooth geometry demands closer control. It also provides a route to correcting limited heat-treatment distortion, provided the part was made with sufficient finishing allowance.


Two hobbed splines can come from very different processes. One may be cut on a rigid modern machine with controlled tooling and established inspection data; another may come from older equipment with substantially more cutter and setup variation. For a close-tolerance shaft, capability data from comparable spline work indicates the capability of the proposed machine and process.


Spline processes by spline type and typical use. Cold rolling work-hardens the surface (Gear Solutions) and leaves compressive residual stress (PartMFG). Grinding gives the closest tolerance and finish and can correct limited heat-treat distortion (PartMFG; GearMFC). Tolerance and finish depend on the machine, tooling and setup, so ask your supplier for capability data from comparable spline work.


## Heat treatment and finishing sequence


Carburized AISI 8620 is common on spline shafts requiring a hard, wear-resistant case with a tougher core. Case hardness around 58 to 62 HRC is used in many applications, with effective case depth selected according to the tooth size and expected loading. Carburized and oil-quenched 8620 typically reaches 58–62 HRC at the case with a 28–40 HRC core, depending on section size (UTEC, citing ASM Handbook Vol. 4A). Select effective case depth for the tooth size and expected loading.


SAE 4140 is frequently induction hardened, where the design calls for localized hardening. Nitriding is also an option, where a hard surface and relatively low process temperature are desirable. Nitriding runs at 500–570 °C with no quench, so distortion stays low, but the case is shallow at about 0.1–0.5 mm (GearMFC). Use it when your loads suit a thin case.


Dimensional planning needs to account for what happens after the teeth are first generated. Carburizing and quenching can distort a long shaft enough to alter spline runout or tooth geometry. If the final spline will be ground, sufficient finishing stock must remain, before hardening.


Case depth has to survive finishing grinding. Removing stock from a carburized surface removes


*case hardened* material, so the specified


*initial* case thickness must allow for this.


Surface hardness checks do not establish case depth. Effective case depth is measured by a microhardness traverse on a sectioned sample. Use a representative coupon or section of a production shaft when that is practical.


## Burrs, finish and coatings


A small burr on a spline flank can be enough to interfere with a close-fitting hub. Deburring methods should therefore remove the raised material without rolling it back onto the working flank. Tooth roots need similar care because damage there can affect fatigue performance.


Cleaning before final gauging is a simple control with a direct effect on the result. Chips or abrasive debris lodged in a tooth space can prevent a functional gauge from entering.


Surface finish should be assigned where it serves a purpose. A working tooth flank and a bearing journal do different jobs, so copying the same roughness requirement across both features is rarely useful.


Coatings need dimensional allowance when their thickness is significant, relative to the spline clearance. For a plated spline, the finished tooth condition should be clear on the drawing and inspection plan. Masking may be preferable where the coating is required elsewhere on the shaft, but would consume too much of the spline fit.


Sliding splines also depend on lubrication and surface condition. Fretting or wear problems are often concentrated in the actual contact region, making the condition of the flank more relevant than a general finish note applied to the whole shaft.


## Misalignment, fretting and fatigue


Angular misalignment shifts spline contact toward one end of the engaged teeth. Local pressure rises in that region, and small relative movement under cyclic torque can produce fretting. Crowning can redistribute the contact, if the expected misalignment is known well enough to design for it.


Repeated, cyclic torque also loads the tooth root and spline runout. A sharp transition or machining mark in the runout can provide a fatigue initiation site while the working flanks still appear relatively undamaged.


The nominal spline length is not a reliable proxy for load distribution. A long engagement with poor alignment can still load a relatively short region heavily. Tooth shear calculations and fatigue assessment need to reflect the geometry actually carrying torque.


Two common spline failure modes. Left: angular misalignment loads one end of the engagement, and micromovement under cyclic torque causes fretting (Ku and Valtierra, as cited in Ratsimba et al., Wear 257, 2004). Right: in a documented vehicle drive-shaft failure, the crack initiated at the spline root (Zhao et al., Engineering Failure Analysis, 2019).


## Inspection through production


A hardened spline should not wait until final inspection for its first meaningful dimensional check.


Measuring right after the spline is cut records what the cutting process produced and gives the supplier a reference for tool wear. After heat treatment, runout or other distortion can be checked before grinding begins. Final analytical measurement and functional gauging then apply to the finished condition that will reach assembly.


For one common hardened-shaft route, the sequence is:


1. Machine


2. Inspect spline


3. Heat treat


4. Inspect distortion and hardness


5. Grind or finish


6. Deburr and clean


7. Analytical inspection


8. Functional gauge


9. Final acceptance


Another process may need fewer stages. An unhardened low-volume shaft, for example, may move directly from spline cutting and deburring to final inspection.


First-piece inspection is primarily a setup check. During a longer run, periodic sample evaluation is needed to reveal drift from cutter wear, or offsets. A supplier that records over-pin dimensions can use the trend itself when deciding when to adjust or replace the cutter.


A first article confirms the setup produced a conforming part. Once enough production data has accumulated, capability analysis can show whether the critical spline characteristic remains centred and sufficiently contained within its tolerance.


## PPAP, AS9102 FAI and traceability


[AS9102C](https://as9100store.com/aerospace-standards-explained/what-is-as9102-first-article-inspection/) s the SAE/IAQG first article inspection standard for aerospace, effective 2023-06-28. It uses three forms and is required under AS9100D clause 8.5.1.3 (New Tech Metals). PPAP is the production part approval process for automotive supply chains, with up to 18 elements depending on the submission level.


Keep the two separate on your drawing notes and PO. An aerospace program asks for AS9102 FAI, and an automotive program asks for PPAP.


The records become useful when a specific result can be followed back through production stages. If final spline runout is out of tolerance, the relevant history includes the machining setup and any distortion introduced by heat treatment. A hardness problem points to the treatment batch and its supporting records.


Material heat, heat-treatment lot and drawing revision are usually among the identifiers valuable to retain for a spline shaft. Gauge identification on the inspection record can also be valuable, when a later investigation raises a question about functional acceptance. Ask for a certificate of conformance (CoC) and material certs with each lot, tied to the material heat and heat-treat lot.


If several lots ship before a problem is found, the heat-treatment and inspection records show which lots went through the affected step or setup. Jiga builds this record chain in: FAI, CoCs, material certs, lot traceability and PPAP on production.


## Supplier qualification before a visit


Initial supplier screening should concentrate on the proposed spline production route. A shop quoting a hobbed external spline should be able to identify the machine and tooling it intends to use, and explain how the spline will be inspected. Comparable spline work is more useful evidence than a general list of CNC machines.


For a shaft with tight spline runout to a bearing journal, review the proposed machining datum and the inspection setup used to measure that runout. A supplier with suitable spline-cutting equipment may still lack a convincing method of holding or verifying the coaxial relationship.


Heat treatment also needs an identified route at the quotation stage, if it can distort the finished geometry. Where the work is subcontracted, the machining supplier still needs a way to preserve lot identity and incorporate the returned parts into final inspection.


For repeat production, representative spline inspection records are worth reviewing before arranging a visit. With Jiga as supplier of record, you start from AS9100, ISO 9001 and ITAR-registered shops, audited continuously and removed when performance drifts.


## Supplier visit validation


At the supplier, follow the proposed shaft through the shop.


Start with the machine and fixtures. Check how the shaft is located and whether the machining datum reflects the functional datum on the drawing. On a shaft where spline runout to a journal is critical, this is usually more revealing than a tour of unrelated high-end equipment.


Then look at the spline inspection equipment being used for comparable work. Functional gauges should have identifiable calibration status. For analytical measurements, ask to see a normal production record and how the result is used to adjust the process.


Heat-treated parts are worth following from dispatch through return and final finishing. Lot identity should survive the outside process. The grinding step needs the case-depth requirement so it doesn’t remove too much hardened material..


Routine production records are worth more time than a prepared first-article example. Look at an ordinary spline batch and see where cutter changes appear in the dimensional record. If an over-pin measurement has drifted, the corresponding offset adjustment, tool change or nonconformance record should be identifiable. Ask for records that span several cutter changes to see whether that control is in use.


## Purchase-order flowdown


The purchase order should carry the drawing revision and the requirements needed to preserve the approved manufacturing route.


Material and heat-treatment specifications are obvious examples. Functional gauging or specific inspection reports also need to appear if they form part of contractual acceptance. Where changing a special-process supplier could alter the validated result, source-change control may need to be included as well.


Repeat orders are where weak flowdown becomes most visible. A drawing may remain unchanged for years, while machines, operators or subcontract heat treaters change. The purchasing information should keep those later batches tied to the same engineering and acceptance requirements.


Where shafts and hubs are sourced separately, the purchase requirements for both components should retain the same spline standard and fit definition. Selective assembly should appear explicitly in the production requirements if the design actually permits it. With Jiga as supplier of record, someone owns this flowdown on every repeat order, and you keep direct access to the shop.

## Frequently Asked Questions


What is the difference between involute and straight-sided splines?


Involute splines use curved involute tooth flanks and have established systems for flank fit, tolerance and functional inspection. Straight-sided splines use substantially parallel flanks. ISO 4156 and DIN 5480 cover involute systems, while ISO 14 covers straight-sided splines with internal centering. Existing mating geometry frequently determines which system should be retained.


How do I specify a spline shaft on an engineering drawing?


Use the complete designation required by the applicable spline standard, including tooth count, pitch or module, pressure angle where applicable, fit and tolerance information. Add usable engagement length, spline termination, datum relationships, runout, heat treatment, coatings and any final-condition inspection requirements that are specific to the shaft rather than supplied by the spline standard.


Are DIN 5480 and ISO 4156 splines interchangeable?


No. DIN 5480 and ISO 4156 are both metric involute spline systems, but they use different design and designation frameworks. DIN 5480 is based on reference diameters and 30° pressure-angle geometry. ISO 4156 is a metric-module side-fit system covering 30°, 37.5° and 45° nominal pressure angles.


How is a spline shaft inspected and accepted?


Inspection commonly combines analytical and functional methods. Measurement over pins or balls provides numerical information about tooth size. A full-form GO gauge evaluates the combined effect of tooth size and relevant geometrical errors on mating. CMM or dedicated spline inspection can add pitch, profile, lead and datum-related information where the drawing requires it.


What material and heat treatment should a high-torque spline shaft use?


Carburized 8620 is common where a hard case and more resilient core are required. 4140 with induction hardening suits many shafts requiring localized hardened surfaces. Nitriding can provide a hard surface with relatively low treatment temperature. Torque, fatigue, wear, case depth, distortion and any required post-treatment grinding determine the better material and treatment route.
